Your phone screen goes completely black when you tilt polarized sunglasses in front of it. LCD screens emit polarized light, and the dark-out is visible on camera.
Your tube light or LED bulb shows rolling dark bands when you film it with your phone camera. The light flickers faster than your eye can see, and the bands show on screen.
Your phone video of a spinning fan or propeller shows bent, wobbling blades. The camera reads the image line by line (rolling shutter), so the blades look warped.
Your phone screen turns into red, green and blue dots when you put a drop of water on it. The drop acts as a magnifier and you see the pixels on camera.
Your selfie camera shows your face mirrored, but the saved photo flips it back. Text on your shirt looks reversed in the preview and normal in the photo.
Your phone's panorama mode can put the same person twice in one photo. Walk behind the camera while it sweeps and the result shows two of you.
Your finger over the phone torch glows red and shows the veins inside it. The light passes through your flesh and you see it on screen.
Your touchscreen reacts to a banana or a fruit tap. Capacitive screens sense anything conductive, so the cursor moves on screen.
Your screenshot of a Netflix or Prime video comes out as a black screen. The apps block screen capture, and the black frame is visible in the gallery.
Your phone camera in Google Lens turns a Hindi or foreign-language sign into English live on screen. The text swaps in real time as you move the camera.
Your humming can name a song. Hum 10 to 15 seconds into the Google app and it lists the matching tracks on screen.
Your Chrome browser hides a dinosaur game that appears when you are offline. Turn off the data, open any page, and tap to play.
Your UPI-style QR code still scans after you scribble over part of it. QR error correction lets a damaged code be read, and you see the scan succeed.
Your phone video of a spinning wheel or fan can show it turning backwards. This wagon-wheel effect appears on camera at the right speed.
Your phone camera on a laptop or TV screen shows a black bar rolling down it. The screen refreshes at a rate that clashes with the camera, and the bar shows on video.
Your phone can copy text out of a photo of a page. Point Google Lens or Live Text at a book and the words become selectable and pasteable on screen.
Your touchscreen goes wild when water drops sit on it. Wet drops confuse the touch sensor, so the screen taps itself on camera.
Your colour newspaper photo is made of tiny dots. Zoom your phone camera in close and the picture breaks into coloured dots.
Your Rs 500 note changes colour when you tilt it. The number 500 shifts from green to blue because of colour-shifting ink.
Your microwave door has a metal mesh full of tiny holes. The holes are small enough to block microwaves while still letting you see the food.
Your FASTag sticker has no battery. A passive RFID tag is powered by the toll reader's radio waves, and the barrier lifts as you pass.
Your gas stove lighter makes a spark with no battery. Squeezing a piezoelectric crystal makes the spark, and you see it jump.
Your solar calculator works with no battery. Cover its small solar panel with your finger and the display fades.
Your plane window has a tiny hole near the bottom. It is a bleed hole that balances pressure between the window panes.
Your chips packet looks puffed up because it is filled with nitrogen. The gas cushions the chips and protects them from spoiling.
Your car's rear windshield has thin lines across the glass. They are heating wires that clear fog and are visible on the glass.
Your induction cooktop can boil water with a sheet of paper under the pan. The magnetic field heats the metal pan itself, so the paper does not burn.
Your smartwatch flashes a green light on the back. It shines on your skin to read your pulse from blood flow.
Your brain can move a computer cursor. Neuralink patients have controlled a cursor by thought, shown in public demo videos.
Your jet suit lets a person fly. Gravity Industries' Richard Browning flies with jet engines on his arms and back, and the footage shows him in the air.
Your hoverboard crossed the sea. Franky Zapata crossed the English Channel on his Flyboard Air in 2019 on his second attempt.
Your sound waves can lift small objects into the air. Acoustic levitation holds droplets and beads floating, visible on camera.
Your drone can be burnt out of the sky by a laser. India's DRDO tested a 30-kilowatt laser weapon in 2025 that brought down drones.
Your artificial sun is real. China's EAST fusion reactor held superheated plasma for 1,066 seconds in January 2025.
Your flying car has flown between two cities. Klein Vision's AirCar flew from Nitra to Bratislava in 2021, with its wings folding out of a car.
Your robot can do a backflip. Boston Dynamics' Atlas humanoid flips in the air, and the video shows it landing on its feet.
Your spacecraft has sailed on sunlight. Japan's IKAROS unfurled a thin square solar sail in 2010, the first to do so in interplanetary space.
Your flame cannot burn a flower sitting on aerogel. This 'frozen smoke' insulates so well that the petals stay safe, and NASA used it to catch comet dust.
Your superconductor can float above a magnet and lock in place. Quantum locking lets it hover, and you can see it hang in mid-air.
Your ferrofluid grows spikes when a magnet comes near. The black liquid forms a spiky pattern, visible on camera.
Your exoskeleton lets a paralysed person stand and walk. Suits like ReWalk show people taking steps in videos.
Your Boeing 787 Dreamliner windows have no shades. The glass dims at the touch of a button and the darkening is visible.
Your blood delivery can arrive by drone. Zipline drones fly medical supplies in Rwanda, dropping them by parachute.
Your airport train floats on magnets. Shanghai's maglev reaches about 430 km/h on a commercial run.
Your hyperloop test track exists in India. IIT Madras built a hyperloop test track, with a pod-and-tube design shown in the footage.
Your taxi has no driver. Waymo's robotaxis carry passengers with nobody in the driver's seat, and the steering wheel turns by itself.
Your face is your boarding pass at some Indian airports. DigiYatra lets you walk through gates with face recognition, and the gate opens on camera.
Your post office was 3D printed. Bengaluru's Cambridge Layout post office was built with a 3D-printing robot, which shows in the building footage.
Your rocket engine can be one single 3D-printed piece. India's Agnikul launched the Agnibaan SOrTeD in 2024 from its own private launchpad at Sriharikota.
Your metro can run with no driver. The Delhi Metro's Magenta Line runs driverless trains, and passengers can stand at the front window.
Your phone screen's single white pixel row turns into red, green and blue stripes under a drop of water, and the on-camera magnified RGB subpixels are the payoff.
Your Rs 10 coin-sized fidget: put a thin sheet of cling film over a phone speaker playing music and sprinkle salt, and the grains dance in patterns you can see (visible sound vibration on any phone).
Your phone's front camera shows the infrared dots of a Face ID-style projector as a purple glow when filmed by a second phone's camera, visible on screen.
Your 4G/Wi-Fi router's blinking LED, filmed in slow-motion on any phone, shows the data pulses as a rapid flicker you can see frame by frame.
Your phone's slow-motion mode at 240 fps shows a ceiling fan's blades frozen and a bulb's AC flicker pulsing, both clearly visible on the screen.

Your credit-card-sized Aadhaar-style QR code is just black and white squares, and a phone camera reads it even when a third of it is covered; the scan succeeds on screen with a marker scribble over it.
Your phone camera filming a CD or DVD surface in sunlight reveals a rainbow spectrum, because the tiny pits act as a diffraction grating, visible on the screen.

Your Ethernet-style USB-C charger plugged into a phone shows 'Charging rapidly' within seconds, but a glass of water with a drop of salt in a sealed bag can't; instead, pour a small ferrofluid-free alternative: a phone placed on a Qi pad lights up while a thin card between them still lets it charge, visible by the charging icon.

Your TV remote's IR LED and your phone camera test already used, so instead: your Rs 20 laser pointer pointed at a CD makes a visible diffraction pattern of dots on the wall, showing the disc's track spacing of about 1.6 micrometres.

Your digital camera in a smartphone sees through thin black plastic: film a bulb through a thin black plastic bag, and near-infrared light passes through so the bulb shows up on screen (works best on some phones, visible on camera).
